prompt.context: You are the SVP of Strategy for Monster.com, a job-search website, at the end of 2005. The US economy is good and you were paid handsomely for the year. You have 3 business lines in the US contributing a total of $600m revenue: 1) Jobs posting business (60%) — list price is $395/posting but with discounting is sold at $60; 2) Resume database business (30%) — sold for $2,000 per user per year (e.g. HR staffer) for access to ~38m resumes; 3) Online pop-up ad business (10%) — e.g. University of Phoenix ad.
prompt.question: Now fast forward to 2009. The CEO has asked you to forecast 2009 US revenues. How will you do it?

clarifying_info.q: What are the underlying drivers of the jobs posting business?
clarifying_info.a: Immediate drivers are US population and unemployment rate; a key driver is job turnover (employees must leave a current position for a job to be posted).

clarifying_info.q: How do we get relevant information for this study?
clarifying_info.a: Sources include US Labor Department, Department of Statistics, online research, Wall Street economic forecasts, etc.

clarifying_info.q: How many people were working in 2005 and 2009, and what was turnover?
clarifying_info.a: In 2005 there were 180m people working and turnover was 20%. There are also 180m people working in 2009. Historical turnover: 1999: 20%, 2001: 10%, 2002: 10%, 2005: 20%.

clarifying_info.q: What is the relationship between turnover and unemployment?
clarifying_info.a: Regression of turnover vs. unemployment showed R-squared of 0.92. Unemployment was 7% in 2001, 3.5% in 2005, and 7% again in 2009.

clarifying_info.q: How many resume database user seats do we expect to sell in 2009?
clarifying_info.a: We expect to sell 60,000 user seats in 2009 at the same $2,000/user price.

clarifying_info.q: What drives the online ad business profitability, and what changed between 2005 and 2009?
clarifying_info.a: Advertiser cost per 1,000 clicks is down 25% in 2009 vs. 2005 due to more competing job sites; however the number of visitors has doubled due to more online users.

framework: Macroeconomy: trends, population growth, unemployment rate and its effect on job turnover
Monster business lines: analyze each of the 3 revenue streams (job postings, resume database, online ads) separately
Competitive dynamics: share gains or losses, emerging competitors, new hiring models
Risks: emerging competitors, new job-search models, pricing pressure
Key insight: biggest challenge is determining what data is important vs. irrelevant; no emerging products or competitive gains to model in this case — focus is on how macro drives each line

questions.prompt: What are the key drivers of the job posting revenue line, and estimate 2009 job posting revenue.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates identify that job postings require employee turnover (someone must leave a job before it is posted). Turnover correlates strongly with the macro economy: high when economy is good, low during recessions. With R-squared of 0.92 vs. unemployment, and unemployment at 7% in 2009 (same as 2001 when turnover was 10%), candidate should estimate 2009 turnover at 10% — half the 2005 rate of 20%. With workers constant at 180m, job postings halve, so revenue halves.

math.setup: 2005 job posting revenue = 60% × $600m = $360m (at 20% turnover). In 2009 turnover = 10% (half of 2005), workers = 180m (unchanged), price constant.
steps: 2009 turnover = 10% (same unemployment 7% as 2001 when turnover was 10%)
Revenue scales proportionally with turnover: 2009 revenue = (10%/20%) × $360m = 0.5 × $360m

questions.guidance: Use the given 60,000 seat estimate at $2,000/user. Calculate and compare to 2005 baseline to note the decline.

questions.prompt: Estimate 2009 online ad revenue given cost-per-1000-clicks is down 25% and visitors doubled.
questions.guidance: Recognize two offsetting effects: price compression from competition (−25%) and volume increase from more internet users (×2). Net effect is 1.5× the 2005 base.

math.setup: 2005 ad revenue = 10% × $600m = $60m. 2009 adjustments: price factor = 0.75; volume factor = 2.0.

questions.prompt: What is total 2009 US revenue and how does it compare to 2005?
questions.guidance: Sum the three lines and compute the percentage decline to give an executive-level conclusion.

math.setup: Sum 2009 revenues across all three lines.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways Monster could sell the resume database differently?

categories.name: Distribution
ideas: White-label database to smaller job boards

recommendation: 2009 US revenue is forecast at $390m, a 35% decline from the $600m recorded in 2005
The primary driver is the macro downturn: higher unemployment suppresses job turnover, directly halving the job-posting business which represents the largest revenue line
risks: Unemployment could worsen further beyond 7%, compressing job-posting revenue below $180m
Accelerating competition from LinkedIn and niche job boards could further erode ad pricing and resume database pricing power
Turnover elasticity model (R-squared 0.92) may not hold perfectly under conditions not seen in the regression window
next_steps: Monitor monthly unemployment data and recalibrate turnover assumptions
Explore resume database re-pricing or bundling to slow the $60m seat decline
Assess whether online ad volume growth (doubled visitors) can be monetized through alternative formats beyond cost-per-click
